title: AI-Assisted Metagenomics Analysis
text:
The datasets
Explore processed taxonomic and functional profiles with Python. Learn one workflow with synthetic practice, repeat it with the hypertension example, then apply it to your own study. Check the inputs, verify the outputs, and explain what the results support.

Hypertension example: current data status



The taxonomic abundances are synthetic placeholders. Their composition and calculated Shannon diversity do not represent the hypertension study. The functional features still require confirmation of their source, definitions and measurement units before biological interpretation. Use this example to practise the workflow while those checks are completed.

title: AI-Assisted Metagenomics Analysis
text:
Start with a guided lesson
Complete Required setup, then work through Synthetic practice in order. Each page explains the task, gives the command to run and shows how to check your work. You will inspect the inputs, generate the figures, verify S01 and write a short report. The functional labels in synthetic practice are fictional identifiers, not real pathway names.
Run commands in your terminal from the main project folder. The guide displays the commands; rendering its pages does not execute the analysis.

title: AI-Assisted Metagenomics Analysis
text:
What you will produce

Taxonomic composition: a stacked bar plot showing within-sample proportions.
Shannon diversity: a plot showing each sample’s calculated diversity and group medians.
Functional profile: a stacked bar plot showing within-sample proportions of the supplied functional features.
Tables and a short report: numerical results you can check and use to support your observations.







Note



Setup is required before running the workflow. Each dataset follows the same page structure, with commands using its own input and output folders. Start with synthetic practice, then repeat the steps with another dataset.


The guide starts from prepared abundance tables. It does not process raw sequencing reads. The outputs are descriptive: visual differences alone do not establish statistical significance or causation, and functional profiles describe the supplied annotations rather than directly measured biological activity.
Next: Set up your workspace

text: Follow steps 1–2 in the project README. Run all commands in a terminal from the main project folder. Quarto is only needed to preview or render the guide and report.

title: Start here
text:
How to use the commands
Run all commands in the terminal, from the main project folder, with the Python environment active. This is the folder containing scripts/, data/ and _quarto.yml.
The code blocks are instructions to copy into your terminal. Rendering the guide does not execute them. When a block starts with python - <<'PY', copy the whole block, including the final PY line: it runs the enclosed Python code in your terminal.
Input files are in data/synthetic/; outputs go to results/synthetic/. Keeping these folders separate helps you trace a result back to its input.
Before you continue: state the question in your own words. What would you need to check before interpreting a similar pattern in a real study?
Next: Preview the results

title: See the result
text:
Composition: what makes up each sample?
First, look at what you will produce. These figures are read from results/synthetic/figures/. If they have not been generated yet, continue through the input checks and analysis, then return here.
Each colour represents a taxon. Its segment height is the taxon’s abundance divided by the sample’s total taxonomic abundance. Every bar sums to 1, or 100%, even when original totals differ.
Compare samples with one large segment against samples with more similarly sized segments. Similar segment sizes indicate more even abundance distributions. Sample order follows the metadata; check group labels before assigning a pattern to A or B.
The script displays up to ten taxa with the highest mean proportions. If more taxa are present, it combines the remainder as Other. The full relative-abundance table retains every taxon.
Try this: pick one bar and identify its largest segment. You will check its numerical proportion later.

title: See the result
text: Figure 4.1: Relative composition of the fictional taxa. Each bar represents one sample.

title: See the result
section: Diversity: how evenly is abundance distributed?
text:
Diversity: how evenly is abundance distributed?






Figure 4.2: Shannon diversity by fictional group. Each dot is a sample; black lines show group medians.



The original lesson describes Group A as having a higher median Shannon diversity and less variation than Group B, with overlap between groups. Confirm that description against your current figure and saved table before using it in your report.

Richness is the number of taxa with abundance greater than zero.
Evenness describes how evenly abundance is distributed among detected taxa.
Shannon diversity combines richness and evenness.

This practice example is expected to have eight detected taxa per sample. Confirm that with the verification code. When richness is the same, differences in Shannon reflect evenness.
The black line is a group’s median, or middle value. Look at the individual dots as well: a median does not describe all variation. Horizontal offsets only separate dots visually. This plot alone does not establish statistical significance.

title: See the result
section: Functions: how are the fictional features distributed?
text:
Functions: how are the fictional features distributed?






Figure 4.3: Relative proportions of fictional functional features. Each bar represents one sample.



Each functional value is divided by the total of the supplied functional values for that sample. A proportion of 0.25 therefore means 25% of that supplied total.
These are invented features, not identified pathways. You can describe their numerical patterns, but cannot infer a named pathway, biological function or measured activity from their labels.

title: See the result
text:
Check your understanding

Can two samples with different original totals have identical proportions? Why?
Can two samples with eight detected taxa have different Shannon values?
Does a larger functional proportion necessarily mean a larger original value?

Ready to continue: you can explain what one bar, one coloured segment, one dot and one median line represent.
Next: Meet the data

title: Meet the data
text:
Understand the layout
The analysis uses three tab-separated text files, or TSVs. A tab separates adjacent columns. Read them with sep="\t" in pandas; do not treat them as comma-separated files.
Samples are rows in metadata and columns in both abundance tables. The same sample IDs connect the files. Spelling and case must match exactly. Renaming a header cannot correct a table that needs to be transposed.

title: Meet the data
text:
Inspect the files yourself
Run this complete block from the main project folder:
python - <<'PY'
from pathlib import Path
import pandas as pd

folder = Path("data/synthetic")
metadata = pd.read_csv(folder / "sample-metadata.tsv", sep="\t")
taxa = pd.read_csv(folder / "taxon-abundance.tsv", sep="\t", index_col=0)
functions = pd.read_csv(folder / "functional-features.tsv", sep="\t", index_col=0)

print("Number of samples:", len(metadata))
print("Taxon table (taxa, samples):", taxa.shape)
print("Functional table (features, samples):", functions.shape)
print("\nSamples per group:")
print(metadata["group"].value_counts().to_string())
print("\nFirst three metadata rows:")
print(metadata.head(3).to_string(index=False))
print("\nTaxon values for S01:")
print(taxa["S01"].to_string())
print("\nFunctional values for S01:")
print(functions["S01"].to_string())
PY
For an abundance table, shape gives (features, samples). Compare its second number with the metadata sample count. Group counts should account for all metadata rows.

title: Meet the data
text:
What do the values mean?
The values are constructed abundance numbers for practice. Do not call their totals sequencing depth, reads, cells or gene copies without documentation that defines them that way. The calculation only needs comparable, nonnegative values within each table and positive sample totals; biological interpretation requires much more context.
A zero means a feature has zero abundance in this practice table. A missing value means the abundance is unknown. Do not replace missing values with zero automatically.
Taxonomic and functional totals have separate denominators. Dividing a functional value by the taxonomic total would calculate the wrong proportion.

title: Meet the data
text:
Your task
Record the number of samples, the number of taxa and functional features, and the group sizes. Locate S01 in all three files. Identify one taxon value and one functional value for that sample.
For a real dataset, you would also need source, units, preprocessing, taxonomic resolution, functional definitions and information about independent participants or repeated samples. Here, all labels and patterns are fictional.

title: Check the inputs
text:
Run the check
Before calculating results, ask whether the three files are consistent and contain usable values. This step prevents avoidable errors from being carried into the figures.
From the main project folder:
--data-dir selects the input folder. --output-dir names the results folder used for a full run. --check-only stops after validation.
The success message follows this pattern:
The sample count should match the number you inspected on the previous page. The angle-bracketed text above is an explanation of the message, not a command or literal output.

python scripts/python/run_workflow.py \
  --data-dir data/synthetic \

title: Check the inputs
text:
What is checked?
The script checks that:

Files have unique headers starting with the required identifier names.
Tables are nonempty, with no blank values or duplicate row identifiers.
Each sample has a nonempty group label.
Sample columns match metadata IDs exactly.
Abundances are numeric, finite and nonnegative.
Every sample has a positive total in each abundance table.

An individual zero is allowed; an all-zero sample cannot be converted to proportions. The script reorders abundance columns to match metadata after checking the IDs.

Do not drop samples or invent values simply to make a check pass. Resolve the source problem and repeat the command.

title: Check the inputs
text:
What does passing mean?
It means the files satisfy the script’s technical requirements. It does not show that a study has a valid design, that samples are independent, or that observed differences are statistically significant.
--check-only creates no new figures and does not refresh existing results. You must run the next step to generate outputs from the checked inputs.
Checkpoint: the check passes, sample and group counts match your notes, and you can explain one problem that validation would catch.

title: Run the analysis
text:
Understand the calculations








Result
Calculation
How to interpret it




Total taxonomic abundance
Sum of taxon values for one sample
Total within the supplied practice table


Detected taxa
Number of taxon values greater than zero
Observed richness within the supplied table


Taxon proportion
Taxon value divided by that sample’s taxon total
A share between 0 and 1


Shannon diversity
\(-\sum_{i:p_i>0}p_i\ln(p_i)\)
Combines richness and evenness; uses the natural logarithm


Functional proportion
Feature value divided by that sample’s functional total
Share of the supplied fictional feature total



Multiplying a proportion by 100 gives a percentage. Taxon proportions and functional proportions each sum to 1 separately for every sample. Shannon uses all supplied taxa, not only those displayed individually in a plot.
For stacked bars, the script displays up to ten features with the highest mean proportions across samples and combines the remainder as Other. This is a display choice, not a test of which features differ between groups.

title: Run the analysis
text:
Inspect before explaining
Open alpha-diversity.tsv, find S01 and record its three calculated values. Then open the figures and return to the preview. Do they show the patterns described there?
The current workflow is descriptive: it performs no hypothesis tests or adjustment for other variables. Functional feature names remain fictional identifiers, not measured biological activities.
Checkpoint: find all three figures and four table/record files, and explain the difference between an original abundance and its proportion.
Next: Verify and explain

title: Verify and explain
text:
1. Check S01 with the supplied script
Verification means tracing a saved number back to the input and checking the calculation yourself. Start with S01, then use tables to support your figure descriptions.
Run from the main project folder:
Record the total taxonomic abundance, detected taxa and natural-log Shannon diversity. Compare them with the S01 row in results/synthetic/tables/alpha-diversity.tsv.

title: Verify and explain
text:
python scripts/python/verify_sample.py \
  data/synthetic results/synthetic S01

title: Verify and explain
text:
2. Recalculate the values independently
Copy this complete block into the terminal. It selects S01, calculates each quantity and compares it with the saved result:
python - <<'PY'
import math
import pandas as pd

sample = "S01"
taxa = pd.read_csv("data/synthetic/taxon-abundance.tsv", sep="\t", index_col=0)
saved = pd.read_csv("results/synthetic/tables/alpha-diversity.tsv", sep="\t", index_col=0)

# Select one sample and calculate its total and observed richness.
x = taxa[sample].astype(float)
total = float(x.sum())
detected = int((x > 0).sum())

# Convert positive values to proportions before calculating Shannon.
p = x[x > 0] / total
shannon = -sum(float(value) * math.log(float(value)) for value in p)

for name, manual in [("total_abundance", total),
                     ("detected_taxa", detected),
                     ("shannon", shannon)]:
    recorded = float(saved.loc[sample, name])
    agrees = math.isclose(manual, recorded, rel_tol=1e-9, abs_tol=1e-9)
    print(f"{name}: manual={manual:.6f}; saved={recorded:.6f}; agrees={agrees}")

# Check a taxon proportion as an additional link to the composition plot.
relative = pd.read_csv("results/synthetic/tables/taxon-relative-abundance.tsv", sep="\t", index_col=0)
taxon = x.idxmax()
manual = x.loc[taxon] / total
recorded = relative.loc[taxon, sample]
print(f"Largest taxon in {sample}: {taxon}; proportion={manual:.6f} ({100 * manual:.2f}%)")
print("Taxon proportion agrees:", math.isclose(manual, recorded, rel_tol=1e-9, abs_tol=1e-9))
PY
All agreement checks should be True. Small final-decimal differences may reflect rounding. Larger discrepancies call for checking the sample ID, input version, most recent run and logarithm base. Do not edit saved values merely to force agreement.
Record your answer: S01 has total …, detected taxa … and Shannon …. My independent calculations [agree/do not agree] with the saved results.

title: Verify and explain
text:
3. Explain richness and evenness
For two equally abundant taxa, proportions are 0.5 and 0.5 and Shannon is approximately 0.6931. For two taxa with proportions 0.9 and 0.1, Shannon is approximately 0.3251. Richness is two in both examples; greater evenness produces the higher Shannon value.
Now check whether richness is constant in this dataset and summarize the groups:
python - <<'PY'
import pandas as pd

alpha = pd.read_csv("results/synthetic/tables/alpha-diversity.tsv", sep="\t")
print("Detected-taxon counts observed:", sorted(alpha["detected_taxa"].unique().tolist()))
summary = alpha.groupby("group", sort=False).agg(
    samples=("shannon", "size"),
    median_shannon=("shannon", "median"),
    minimum_shannon=("shannon", "min"),
    maximum_shannon=("shannon", "max"),
    sd_shannon=("shannon", "std"),
)
print(summary.round(6).to_string())
PY
The original lesson expects all samples to have eight detected taxa. If the output confirms [8], Shannon differences reflect evenness. If it does not, investigate the input version and revise that explanation: richness may also contribute.
Use medians to compare typical values and ranges or standard deviations to describe variation. Standard deviation summarizes spread around a group’s mean; it is not an uncertainty interval for the median. Neither summary establishes statistical significance.

title: Verify and explain
text:
4. Check one functional proportion
This example selects the first fictional feature in the input file. It checks the arithmetic without assuming a biological meaning for that label:
python - <<'PY'
import math
import pandas as pd

sample = "S01"
raw = pd.read_csv("data/synthetic/functional-features.tsv", sep="\t", index_col=0)
saved = pd.read_csv("results/synthetic/tables/functional-relative-abundance.tsv", sep="\t", index_col=0)
feature = raw.index[0]
value = float(raw.loc[feature, sample])
total = float(raw[sample].sum())
manual = value / total
recorded = float(saved.loc[feature, sample])
print(f"{feature}: value={value:g}; functional total={total:g}")
print(f"Calculated proportion={manual:.6f} ({100 * manual:.2f}%)")
print(f"Saved proportion={recorded:.6f}")
print("Agrees:", math.isclose(manual, recorded, rel_tol=1e-9, abs_tol=1e-9))
PY
A larger proportion can result from a larger feature value, smaller values for other features, or both. These plots show relative distributions within the supplied feature set.

title: Verify and explain
text:
5. Write observations with evidence
Return to the three figures and complete one observation for each:







Figure
Include in your observation




Composition
Sample ID, fictional taxon ID and checked proportion


Shannon diversity
Group medians, spread, overlap and detected-taxon counts


Functional profile
Fictional feature ID, sample ID and checked proportion



Example wording: “Group … has a calculated median Shannon of …, compared with … in Group …. The distributions overlap. All samples have … detected taxa, so …. These descriptive results do not establish statistical significance.”
Keep a short evidence note for each statement: the table used, numerical value and limitation. If you ask AI to help draft an explanation, provide those checked values and review every claim yourself.
Ready to report: you can reproduce S01’s results and explain the patterns without assigning real pathway names or claiming causation.
Next: Write the report

title: Export the report
text:
Create or update the report
A report connects the question, calculations and observations. Keep it short enough to follow, but include the evidence needed to check your claims.
Open reports/synthetic-report.qmd. If it does not exist, create it in the reports/ folder. Use the template below, replacing every square-bracketed prompt with your own checked results.
The figure paths are relative to the report’s location in reports/. They differ from paths used in the lesson pages.

title: Export the report
text:

title: See the result
text:
Taxonomic composition: how is abundance distributed?
Start by learning how to read the outputs. The figures below come from results/hypertension/figures/. If they have not been generated yet, continue through the input checks and analysis, then return here.
Each bar sums to 1, or 100%. A coloured segment shows one taxon’s share of that sample’s total abundance. The workflow displays the ten taxa with the highest mean within-sample proportions across all samples; remaining taxa are combined as Other.
A taller segment means a larger proportion, not necessarily a larger absolute abundance. The samples follow metadata order; the plot does not explicitly label group boundaries. Use the metadata and saved table before assigning a pattern to a group.
Look for: samples dominated by a few taxa and samples with more evenly sized segments. Describe variation without treating fictional taxon names as biological organisms.

title: See the result

title: See the result
section: Shannon diversity: richness and evenness together
text:
Shannon diversity: richness and evenness together






Figure 11.2: Calculated Shannon diversity by metadata group. Each dot is one sample; black lines show group medians.




Richness here means the number of taxa with abundance greater than zero.
Evenness describes how evenly abundance is distributed among those taxa.
Shannon diversity combines both properties. A higher value can reflect more detected taxa, more even abundances, or both.

The vertical position of each dot is its calculated Shannon value. Horizontal offsets only separate samples visually. Read the median lines together with the spread and overlap of the dots; the plot contains no hypothesis test.
Think about: could two samples with 12 detected taxa have different Shannon values? Yes: their abundances can be distributed differently.

title: See the result
section: Functional profile: proportions within the supplied feature set
text:
Functional profile: proportions within the supplied feature set






Figure 11.3: Within-sample proportions of the supplied functional features. Each bar is one sample; remaining features are combined as Other.



The script divides each functional value by the sum of the supplied functional values for that sample. It displays the ten features with the highest mean proportions and combines the remainder as Other.
A value of 0.20 therefore means 20% of this supplied feature total. It is not automatically 20% of all microbial functions, genes or sequencing reads. Feature definitions, units and possible overlap must be understood before interpreting these proportions biologically. The plot does not directly measure biological activity.

title: Check the inputs
text:
What the script checks

Required files have unique headers beginning with sample_id, taxon_id or feature_id, as appropriate.
Tables are nonempty, with no blank cells or duplicate row identifiers.
Metadata has a nonempty group value for every sample.
Sample columns in each abundance table match metadata sample IDs exactly.
Abundances are numeric, finite and nonnegative, with a positive total for every sample in each abundance table.

Zero abundance for an individual feature is allowed. An all-zero sample is rejected because it cannot be normalized to proportions.

title: Run the analysis
text:
Understand the calculations
Taxonomic composition: divide each taxon’s abundance by that sample’s total taxonomic abundance. The resulting proportions sum to 1.
Detected taxa: count taxon values greater than zero. This is richness within the supplied table, not an estimate of all organisms present.
Shannon diversity: calculate \(H = -\sum_{i:p_i>0}p_i\ln(p_i)\), where \(p_i\) is a taxon’s within-sample proportion. Zero values do not contribute. The script uses the natural logarithm.
Functional profile: separately divide each functional value by that sample’s supplied functional-feature total. Taxonomic and functional totals are different denominators and should not be compared as if they were the same quantity.
Both stacked bar plots display the ten features with the highest mean proportions across samples and combine remaining features into Other. This selection is for display, not a statistical test. Shannon uses all supplied taxa, including those combined as Other in the figure.

title: Verify and explain

Quantity
Expected value




Total taxonomic abundance
4,761


Detected taxa
12


Shannon diversity, natural logarithm
2.202635




python scripts/python/verify_sample.py \
  data/hypertension results/hypertension ERR1398068


Recalculate independently
This block makes each calculation visible and compares it with the saved row. Copy the complete block into the terminal:
python - <<'PY'
import math
import pandas as pd

sample = "ERR1398068"
taxa = pd.read_csv("data/hypertension/taxon-abundance.tsv", sep="\t", index_col=0)
saved = pd.read_csv("results/hypertension/tables/alpha-diversity.tsv", sep="\t", index_col=0)

# Calculate this sample's total and number of positive taxon values.
x = taxa[sample].astype(float)
total = float(x.sum())
detected = int((x > 0).sum())

# Only positive values contribute to natural-log Shannon diversity.
p = x[x > 0] / total
shannon = -sum(float(value) * math.log(float(value)) for value in p)

for name, manual in [("total_abundance", total),
                     ("detected_taxa", detected),
                     ("shannon", shannon)]:
    recorded = float(saved.loc[sample, name])
    agrees = math.isclose(manual, recorded, rel_tol=1e-9, abs_tol=1e-9)
    print(f"{name}: manual={manual:.6f}; saved={recorded:.6f}; agrees={agrees}")
PY
All three comparisons should print agrees=True. A tiny difference in the last decimal places can be rounding. A larger difference calls for checking the input version, selected sample, normalization and logarithm base. Do not change a saved result merely to make it agree.
source_shannon_index is a separate supplied metadata field. It is not the reference value for this calculation from placeholder taxa.

title: Verify and explain
text:
2. Check a functional proportion
For ERR1398068, the supplied functional values sum to 45,300 and LPS_biosynthesis is 436. The saved proportion should therefore be approximately \(436/45300 = 0.009625\), or 0.9625% of the supplied functional total.
python - <<'PY'
import math
import pandas as pd

sample = "ERR1398068"
feature = "LPS_biosynthesis"
raw = pd.read_csv("data/hypertension/functional-features.tsv", sep="\t", index_col=0)
saved = pd.read_csv("results/hypertension/tables/functional-relative-abundance.tsv", sep="\t", index_col=0)
manual = raw.loc[feature, sample] / raw[sample].sum()
recorded = saved.loc[feature, sample]
print(f"Calculated proportion: {manual:.6f} ({100 * manual:.4f}%)")
print(f"Saved proportion:      {recorded:.6f}")
print("Agrees:", math.isclose(manual, recorded, rel_tol=1e-9, abs_tol=1e-9))
PY
This checks arithmetic. It does not establish what the original feature values measure or whether their sum is a biologically appropriate denominator.

3. Explain taxonomic composition






Figure 15.1: Composition calculated from synthetic placeholder taxa. Each bar represents one sample.



Choose one sample with an uneven profile. Use taxon-relative-abundance.tsv to identify its largest taxon proportion, then write a sentence containing the sample ID, taxon ID and value. Other combines taxa rather than naming an organism.
Sentence starter: “In sample …, placeholder taxon … accounts for …% of the supplied taxonomic abundance.” This describes the exercise without implying a hypertension association.

title: Verify and explain
text:
4. Explain Shannon diversity






Figure 15.2: Shannon diversity calculated from placeholder taxa. Each dot is a sample; black lines indicate group medians.



Inspect sample counts, spread and overlap before comparing medians. Generate a numerical summary:
python - <<'PY'
import pandas as pd

alpha = pd.read_csv("results/hypertension/tables/alpha-diversity.tsv", sep="\t")
summary = alpha.groupby("group", sort=False).agg(
    samples=("shannon", "size"),
    median_shannon=("shannon", "median"),
    minimum_shannon=("shannon", "min"),
    maximum_shannon=("shannon", "max"),
    minimum_detected_taxa=("detected_taxa", "min"),
    maximum_detected_taxa=("detected_taxa", "max"),
)
print(summary.round(6).to_string())
PY
In the current placeholder table, samples have 11 or 12 detected taxa. Do not assume richness is identical throughout. For two samples with the same detected-taxon count, a Shannon difference reflects evenness; across samples with different counts, both richness and evenness may contribute.
Your task: identify the group with the highest calculated median, quote the value and describe overlap with the other groups. Add: “These values were calculated from synthetic placeholder taxa and do not establish a study finding or statistical significance.”

Taxonomic and functional values were separately divided by their respective
within-sample totals. Detected taxa had values greater than zero.
Shannon diversity used all supplied taxa and the natural logarithm.
Stacked bar plots display the ten features with the highest mean
proportions, with the remainder combined as Other. The analysis was descriptive.

## Verification

4,761, 12 detected taxa and Shannon diversity 2.202635.
[State whether these values agreed with the saved results.]

For this sample, LPS_biosynthesis was 436 out of a supplied functional
total of 45,300: a proportion of approximately 0.009625.
[State whether this agreed with the saved functional table.]

title: See the result
text:
How to read the figures
Stacked bars: each bar is a sample and each segment is a feature’s share of that sample’s supplied total. A bar sums to 1, even when original sample totals differ. A larger proportion does not necessarily mean a larger absolute abundance. The workflow displays up to ten features with the highest mean proportions and combines remaining features as Other.
Diversity dots: each dot is a sample and its vertical position is its Shannon diversity. Horizontal offsets separate dots visually. Black lines mark group medians. Read these together with the individual values, detected-taxon counts and overlap. With one group, describe sample variation rather than a group comparison.
Functional profiles: proportions use only the supplied feature total as their denominator. Confirm that the features are comparable and understand whether categories overlap. A functional label or abundance estimate is not direct evidence of activity.
Samples in stacked bars follow metadata order. Group boundaries are not explicitly labelled, so check the metadata before assigning a section of bars to a group.

Use these filenames and headers
Prepare working copies of your inputs in data/my-study/. A TSV is a plain-text table with tabs between columns. Changing a filename from .csv to .tsv does not change its separator; export it as tab-separated text.
Samples are rows in metadata and columns in the abundance tables. Each sample ID must appear once in metadata and once as a column header in each abundance table. Keep identifiers as text so leading zeros are preserved. IDs are case-sensitive: S01 and s01 differ.
If you have one descriptive group, use a meaningful label such as All_samples. Do not invent comparison groups. If your data include transformations with negative values, return to an appropriate nonnegative abundance representation rather than deleting negative values.
A zero means zero in the supplied table; a missing value means unknown. Do not replace missing values with zero without justification. Optional metadata columns must also have nonblank values to pass the current validator; record an explicit missingness label or omit an optional column where appropriate, and document the decision. Do not fabricate measurements.

title: Run the analysis
text:
Inspect your first run

Open alpha-diversity.tsv and check that sample IDs and groups are yours.
Locate the three figures and inspect their axes and legends.
Return to See the result to display your figures in the guide if desired.
Keep the exact inputs and provenance notes with your analysis. The run record does not include input checksums or every preparation decision.

With many samples, labels may overlap. That is a presentation problem rather than evidence of an incorrect calculation. Use saved tables for sample-specific checks and adapt plotting labels separately if needed.
The workflow is descriptive. It does not account for repeated samples, adjust for confounding variables or test group differences. A functional profile does not directly measure activity.
Checkpoint: all seven output files exist and contain results from your study. Now verify a sample before interpreting patterns.

title: Verify and explain
text:
1. Choose a sample
Choose one sample, calculate its results directly from the input and compare them with the saved outputs. This both checks the workflow and shows you how the calculations work in Python.
There are no fixed numerical answers for your study. Your independent calculation and saved result should agree when they use the same inputs and method.
Run this short block to list the first ten sample IDs:
Choose an ID and copy it exactly. In the command below, replace YOUR_SAMPLE_ID with that ID. Keep the quotation marks; they help if the ID contains spaces.
Record the reported total, detected taxa and Shannon value. Compare them with the corresponding row in results/my-study/tables/alpha-diversity.tsv.

title: Verify and explain
text:
2. See the calculations in Python
The code below uses the first metadata sample automatically, so it can run without editing. It prints the chosen ID. To use the ID you selected above, replace the sample = ... line with sample = "your actual ID".
Copy the entire block, from python - <<'PY' through the final PY, into your terminal:
python - <<'PY'
import math
import pandas as pd

metadata = pd.read_csv("data/my-study/sample-metadata.tsv", sep="\t", dtype=str, keep_default_na=False)
sample = metadata.loc[0, "sample_id"]
print("Verifying sample:", sample)

taxa = pd.read_csv("data/my-study/taxon-abundance.tsv", sep="\t", index_col=0)
saved = pd.read_csv("results/my-study/tables/alpha-diversity.tsv", sep="\t", dtype={"sample_id": str}, keep_default_na=False).set_index("sample_id")

# Select the sample's values and calculate its total and richness.
x = taxa[sample].astype(float)
total = float(x.sum())
detected = int((x > 0).sum())

# Use positive proportions for natural-log Shannon diversity.
p = x[x > 0] / total
shannon = -sum(float(value) * math.log(float(value)) for value in p)

for name, manual in [("total_abundance", total),
                     ("detected_taxa", detected),
                     ("shannon", shannon)]:
    recorded = float(saved.loc[sample, name])
    agrees = math.isclose(manual, recorded, rel_tol=1e-9, abs_tol=1e-9)
    print(f"{name}: manual={manual:.6f}; saved={recorded:.6f}; agrees={agrees}")

# Check the largest taxon's proportion against the saved table.
relative = pd.read_csv("results/my-study/tables/taxon-relative-abundance.tsv", sep="\t", index_col=0)
taxon = x.idxmax()
manual = x.loc[taxon] / total
recorded = float(relative.loc[taxon, sample])
print(f"Largest taxon: {taxon}; proportion={manual:.6f} ({100 * manual:.2f}%)")
print("Taxon proportion agrees:", math.isclose(manual, recorded, rel_tol=1e-9, abs_tol=1e-9))

# Separately check the first supplied functional feature.
functions = pd.read_csv("data/my-study/functional-features.tsv", sep="\t", index_col=0)
functional_saved = pd.read_csv("results/my-study/tables/functional-relative-abundance.tsv", sep="\t", index_col=0)
feature = functions.index[0]
manual = float(functions.loc[feature, sample]) / float(functions[sample].sum())
recorded = float(functional_saved.loc[feature, sample])
print(f"Functional feature: {feature}; proportion={manual:.6f} ({100 * manual:.2f}%)")
print("Functional proportion agrees:", math.isclose(manual, recorded, rel_tol=1e-9, abs_tol=1e-9))
PY

What the key lines do







Code
Meaning




taxa[sample]
Select one sample column


x.sum()
Add the taxon values


(x > 0).sum()
Count detected taxa


x[x > 0] / total
Convert positive taxon values to proportions


math.log(value)
Take the natural logarithm


math.isclose(...)
Compare numbers while allowing tiny rounding differences



All agreement checks should be True. This supports the checked calculations for that sample; it does not validate every sample or establish a biological conclusion.
If a check is False, check the selected sample, input version, output folder and whether results were regenerated after editing inputs. Do not change saved values to force agreement. If necessary, inspect the original data and rerun validation and analysis.

title: Verify and explain
text:
3. Summarize your diversity values
python - <<'PY'
import pandas as pd

alpha = pd.read_csv("results/my-study/tables/alpha-diversity.tsv", sep="\t", dtype={"sample_id": str, "group": str}, keep_default_na=False)
summary = alpha.groupby("group", sort=False).agg(
    samples=("shannon", "size"),
    median_shannon=("shannon", "median"),
    minimum_shannon=("shannon", "min"),
    maximum_shannon=("shannon", "max"),
    minimum_detected_taxa=("detected_taxa", "min"),
    maximum_detected_taxa=("detected_taxa", "max"),
)
print(summary.round(6).to_string())
PY
Compare group medians, variation and overlap. If there is only one group, describe variation among its samples.
Richness versus evenness: when two samples have the same number of detected taxa, a difference in Shannon reflects evenness. When detected-taxon counts differ, both may contribute. Do not assume every sample has the same richness because the input table has a fixed number of rows.

title: Verify and explain
text:
4. Turn observations into supported statements







Output
A useful observation includes




Composition
Sample ID, taxon name/ID and a checked proportion


Diversity
Group medians or sample values, detected-taxon counts and overlap


Functional profile
Feature ID/definition, proportion, denominator and relevant units



For each figure, write: what I see; the number supporting it; what I cannot conclude; what I would check next.
For example: “Sample … has …% of the supplied taxonomic abundance assigned to …. This is a relative proportion and does not directly establish the absolute amount present.”
Do not infer significance or causation from plots. Check group sizes, repeated samples, processing differences and relevant covariates before deciding what additional statistical analysis is appropriate. If a source diversity value is present in metadata, keep it separate from the value calculated here unless the input profiles and methods are known to match.
If you ask AI to help explain a figure, supply the checked values and units, then review each statement yourself.
Ready to report: you have recorded the chosen ID, checked values, agreement results and one supported observation for each figure.
Next: Write the report

text:

Your report should let another person understand the question, trace the evidence and see the limits of the analysis. Use your own values; do not carry answers over from synthetic practice or hypertension.
Create reports/my-study-report.qmd in your editor. Copy this template and replace every square-bracketed prompt. The figure paths are correct for a report saved in reports/.

title: Appendix A — Appendix
text:
Shannon diversity
For positive taxon proportions \(p_i\), \(H=-\sum_i p_i\ln(p_i)\). Zero proportions contribute zero. Detected taxa count features with abundance greater than zero. Total abundance is the sum of the supplied units, not necessarily read depth.

title: Appendix A — Appendix
text:
Functional profiles
Feature abundance, pathway abundance, and pathway coverage have different meanings. Confirm the source units and feature definitions before deciding whether within-sample normalization is appropriate. This starter requires an abundance-like matrix with positive sample totals.
